planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, well-drained sand or gravelly soil so winter cold and moisture can break seed dormancy; plants spend their first one to two seasons as a low, spiny basal rosette before sending up a flowering stalk.

directions: Hill's thistle is a short, woolly-stemmed native thistle that stays compact compared to most of its relatives, topping out well under two feet with one or a few large, fragrant pink-purple flower heads that draw bumblebees and butterflies. It is a true specialist of dry, open, calcium-rich ground, turning up on sand barrens, dry prairie knolls, and limestone alvar openings around the western Great Lakes rather than in rich garden soil. Because it resents competition and root disturbance, it is best direct-seeded in place in a lean, sun-baked bed and then left largely alone rather than transplanted as an older plant. Unlike the introduced bull and Canada thistles it is often confused with, it is a well-behaved, non-aggressive native that does not need to be removed.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or plugs in spring directly into loose, shifting beach sand; set them in staggered clusters rather than a single row so the spreading rhizomes can begin knitting the dune surface together quickly.

directions: American dune grass is a stout, blue-green, strongly rhizomatous grass that colonizes active foredunes on the Great Lakes as well as the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, sending roots deep into loose sand to anchor shifting slopes. It tolerates salt spray, burial by blowing sand, and prolonged summer drought, and actually grows more vigorously when periodically covered with fresh sand than when left undisturbed. In restoration plantings it is typically set out as rooted plugs rather than seeded, since young seedlings establish slowly compared to divisions taken from an existing stand. Once established it spreads aggressively by rhizome, so give it room on an open dune or beachfront slope rather than a contained garden bed.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold-stratify and plant plugs in spring into loose, open, calcareous beach sand with little competing vegetation; this goldenrod is adapted to the moving, nutrient-poor sand of an active dune rather than a mulched perennial bed.

directions: Gillman's goldenrod is a low, often sprawling variety of early goldenrod that grows almost nowhere but open sand dunes along Lakes Michigan, Huron, and Superior, where its thick, fleshy, somewhat succulent leaves and stems resist burial and desiccation on exposed beach ridges. It flowers later in the season than most dune plants, producing dense, showy clusters of bright yellow blooms in the back dune and foredune zone where few other perennials persist. Give it full sun and sharply draining sand with no fertilizer or irrigation once established, since rich or consistently moist soil favors taller competitors that quickly crowd it out. It is state-listed as threatened in parts of its range, so source only nursery-propagated seed or divisions rather than wild-collected material.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into damp, calcium-rich, gravelly soil along a sunny shoreline flat or alvar swale; keep the site reliably moist through the growing season rather than letting it dry out like a true pavement sedge.

directions: Garber's sedge forms small, neat tufts of narrow green leaves topped by short spikes in late spring, growing naturally along cold, calcareous lakeshores, wet alvar swales, and interdunal flats around the upper Great Lakes. It needs steadier moisture than the dry-pavement sedges it often grows near, favoring seepy gravel bars and damp shoreline flats over the baking-hot bare rock of a true alvar crest. In a garden setting it fits a constructed fen, pond margin, or damp gravel bed built over limestone screenings, paired with other small calciphile sedges and shoreline forbs. Clumps increase slowly by short rhizomes and can be divided every few years to spread a planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently wet, calcareous, mucky-to-gravelly soil such as a marl fen edge or shoreline seep in full to partial sun; this is a true wet-ground sedge and will not persist in a dry rock garden setting.

directions: Little green sedge is a small, loosely tufted sedge with bright yellow-green, globe-shaped seed heads that stand out against the surrounding vegetation of the calcareous fens, marly shoreline seeps, and wet alvar swales it favors around the Great Lakes. It is one of the smallest sedges typical of these habitats, often rooting directly in saturated marl or thin, mineral soil that would drown most other perennials. In cultivation it belongs in a constructed fen bed or the saturated margin of a pond built over limestone gravel, kept wet through the growing season rather than allowed to dry between waterings. It spreads gradually into loose colonies and is easiest to establish from nursery-grown divisions set directly into permanently damp ground.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, damp, calcareous soil, since seed needs light and winter cold-moist stratification to germinate; plants form a basal rosette the first year and bloom in their second year before setting seed and dying back.

directions: Lesser fringed gentian sends up slender, erect stems topped with narrow, deep blue, delicately fringed flowers that open in late summer and fall, closing again each night and on cloudy days. It grows naturally in calcareous fens, wet alvar-margin meadows, and damp shoreline flats across the Great Lakes region and southern Canada, favoring open, mineral-rich ground kept constantly moist by groundwater seepage. As a biennial, it depends on bare patches of damp soil for its seedlings to establish each year, so a planting needs some light disturbance or thin mulch rather than a dense, closed groundcover. Once a colony is going, letting some flowers go to seed each fall is the simplest way to keep the population self-sustaining from year to year.
